blocks.prompt: The Pump in Your Chest
blocks.text: Your heart is a pump. A pump pushes things along. Your heart pushes blood. Blood carries food and air to every part of you, all the way down to your toes. Put your ear on a grown-up's chest and listen. You will hear lub-dub, lub-dub. That is the sound of little doors closing inside the heart. The doors keep the blood going one way, like a one-way street. Now run around the yard ten times. Stop and feel your chest. Your heart is going faster. Your muscles want more air, so your heart works harder to bring it.

blocks.prompt: The Pump in Your Chest
blocks.text: Your heart is not shaped like the heart on a greeting card. It is a lumpy bag of muscle about the size of your fist, and it sits in the middle of your chest with its tip pointed a little to the left. That is why people think it lives on the left side. The heart has one job. It pushes blood. Blood is a delivery truck: it carries oxygen from your lungs and food from your stomach out to every muscle and bone you own, then hauls the trash back. Your heart pushes it around this loop again and again, about 100,000 times a day, without you asking it to. Inside the heart are four little doors called valves. When you hear lub-dub through a stethoscope, you are not hearing blood. You are hearing those doors slam shut. They snap closed so blood cannot slosh backward. Every drop has to keep moving one way around the loop. Your heart also listens to you. Sit still and it slows down. Run up a hill and it speeds up, because your legs are shouting for more oxygen and the heart is the only thing that can deliver it.

4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: Two Pumps in One
blocks.text: Hold up your fist. Your heart is about that size, and it is made almost entirely of muscle. Unlike the muscles in your arm, this one never gets to quit. Most people picture the heart as a single pump. It is really two pumps bolted together, working side by side. The right pump takes tired blood coming back from your body and sends it on a short trip to your lungs, where it picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide. The refreshed blood returns to the left pump, which fires it out to the rest of you: brain, fingers, stomach, toes. The left pump has the harder job, so its wall is nearly three times thicker than the right. Each pump has two rooms, an upper one and a lower one, which is why doctors say the heart has four chambers. Between the rooms sit valves, flaps of tissue that open one way only. Their snapping shut is the lub-dub you hear through a stethoscope. Here is the strange part. The heart is stuffed with blood every second of its life, yet it cannot use a drop of it. The walls are too thick to soak anything up. So the heart feeds itself the same way it feeds everything else: through its own private vessels, the coronary arteries, which branch across its surface like a tree pressed onto the muscle. One more thing. Blood is never blue. Blood without much oxygen is a deep, dark red. Your veins only look blue because of the way light passes through your skin.

notes: Cardiac muscle makes its own electricity

blocks.prompt: The Heart Beats Itself
blocks.text: Here is a fact that should bother you more than it does. Your heart does not wait for your brain to tell it to beat. Almost every muscle you own is a puppet. Your bicep does nothing until a nerve signal arrives from your brain. Cut that nerve and the muscle goes quiet forever. Cardiac muscle refuses to work that way. The heart generates its own beat, from inside itself, using electricity it makes on the spot. The spark starts in a patch of specialized cells in the upper right chamber called the sinoatrial node. Doctors call it the natural pacemaker. Roughly once a second, all on its own schedule, the sinoatrial node leaks a small electrical charge across the two upper chambers, and they squeeze. The charge pauses briefly at a second checkpoint, the atrioventricular node, long enough for the upper chambers to finish emptying. Then it races down into the two lower chambers, and they squeeze harder, throwing blood to the lungs and to the body. That whole sequence, repeated, is a heartbeat. If you want proof that the heart runs itself, look at a transplant. When surgeons place a donor heart into a patient's chest, they do not reconnect the nerves that once ran to it. They cannot. The heart beats anyway, from the first minute, because the sinoatrial node inside it has never needed instructions from anyone's brain. Your brain does still get a vote. It cannot start the beat, but it can lean on the pace, speeding the heart up when you sprint and slowing it down when you settle. Think of the sinoatrial node as a drummer who never stops drumming, and the brain as a conductor who can only ask for faster or slower. None of this is free. Cardiac muscle burns oxygen constantly and stores almost nothing in reserve. Block the coronary arteries feeding it and the muscle downstream begins to die within minutes. The organ that keeps every other organ alive is the least forgiving one you have.

6.title: The Pump That Never Quits
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Galen taught that the liver made blood and the body used it up
Harvey's proof was arithmetic, not a microscope
De Motu Cordis, 1628, about 70 pages
Malpighi saw the capillaries in 1661
Roughly 2,000 gallons of blood moved a day

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Counted the Blood
blocks.text: For fourteen hundred years, European doctors believed that blood was food. The theory came from Galen, a Greek physician who treated Roman gladiators and whose word went essentially unquestioned until the 1600s. In Galen's system, the liver manufactured fresh blood out of digested meals and sent it outward through the veins, where the body's tissues soaked it up and consumed it, the way a lamp consumes oil. Blood was made, delivered, and used up. More was made tomorrow. The heart, in this picture, was not really a pump. It was a furnace that warmed the blood and stirred it. William Harvey, an English doctor trained in Italy, killed that idea with arithmetic. Harvey did not begin with a microscope or a grand theory. He began by measuring. He opened hearts and estimated how much blood the left chamber held, then multiplied by how often the heart beat. Even using deliberately cautious numbers, the answer was absurd. The heart pushed out more than the weight of a whole person in blood every hour. The liver could not possibly manufacture that. No meal could supply it. If blood were consumed the way Galen said, a body would need to eat itself several times over before lunch. There was only one way out of the arithmetic. The blood was not being used up at all. It was going around, the same blood, over and over, in a closed circle. Harvey then went looking for the plumbing that a circle would require. He tied off arteries and watched them swell on the side nearest the heart, which meant blood flowed outward through them. He pressed on the veins in a volunteer's arm and found the little valves inside would only let blood travel one direction, toward the heart. He could not see the microscopic vessels linking the two systems, because the lens to see them did not yet exist, and he said so plainly rather than inventing an answer. Four years after Harvey died, Marcello Malpighi put a frog's lung under a microscope and found the capillaries exactly where the arithmetic had insisted they must be. When Harvey published his findings in 1628, in a thin book called De Motu Cordis, the reaction was not applause. Colleagues called him crackbrained. His medical practice shrank. It took roughly twenty years for the profession to concede that a man with a scale and a multiplication problem had overturned fourteen centuries of authority. This is worth sitting with. Harvey's evidence was not exotic. Anyone in Galen's era could have done the same multiplication, using the same hearts and the same clock. Nobody did, because nobody thought the question was open. What Harvey actually contributed was not a discovery so much as a refusal: he checked a number that everyone else had agreed not to check. Your heart moves roughly two thousand gallons of blood a day through something like sixty thousand miles of vessels, and it does this by pushing the same few quarts around a loop, endlessly. You know that only because one stubborn man did the math and trusted it more than he trusted Galen.
